item.title: Dakar 2026 Youth Olympics opens in historic first for Africa
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-01
Photo shows the Olympic rings during the opening ceremony of the 2026 Youth Olympic Games in Dakar, Senegal, Oct. 31, 2026. (Xinhua/Chen Wei) DAKAR, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- The Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games (YOG) opened on Saturday, marking the first time an Olympic event has been held on African soil. The opening ceremony took place at the 55,000-seat Abdoulaye Wade Stadium in Diamniadio, a new city located 30 km from Senegal's capital of Dakar. According to the organizing committee, Khady Niang, the ceremony director, said the show allows Africa to "tell the world who we are, where we come from and where we want to go." The two-hour show started at 6:30 p.m. local time, marked by the arrival of International Olympic Committee President Kirsty Coventry and Senegalese President Bassirou Diomaye Faye. Following the parade of athletes, the spotlight turned to a story of three generations passing the baton from one to the next: Alkebulan, the mother, represented the values of ancestral Africa; her son, Keb, embodied Africa today; and Sitoe, a young Senegalese girl, symbolized hope for the future. The opening act paid tribute to the Africa of the past, immediately electrifying the crowd as Alkebulan rode into the arena on horseback. Iconic instruments, including the sabar, the tama (talking drum) and the djembe, introduced the continent's rich musical heritage, while traditional attire from Mali, Ghana, Senegal and South Africa showcased the diversity of African cultural traditions. The momentum built with performances of Senegal's traditional faux-lion dance and wrestlers' dance, culminating in a finale in which 360 dancers came together to form the map of Africa. In the second act, Keb arrived on a motorcycle in a scene inspired by the Senegalese film Touki Bouki. He led Sitoe and the spectators into the world of contemporary African art, striking a chord with younger generations. As Keb and Sitoe strolled through the streets, a series of artistic performances featuring live painting, music, dance and hip-hop brought the scene to life. The festivities were followed by the parade of flags representing the participating national Olympic committees, with Greece and the Refugee Olympic Team leading the procession and host nation Senegal bringing up the rear. "For years, we have been talking about this moment -- the first Olympic sporting event on African soil and now here we are. This historic moment is for Senegal, for Africa, for our entire Olympic movement, and to all of our young amazing athletes," Coventry said in her speech. "This is the Africa that I am so proud and so excited for the world to experience," she added, voicing hope for young talents to "believe in yourselves, to dream big and to do things you never thought were possible." After Senegalese President Faye officially declared the fourth Summer Youth Olympic Games open, the stadium erupted in vibrant Afrobeats music. The celebration continued with sports demonstrations, a choreographed formation of the Olympic rings and the Dakar 2026 emblem, the Olympic anthem, the raising of the Olympic flag and the solemn reading of the Youth Olympic oath. The much-anticipated lighting of the Olympic cauldron came last. Senegalese fencer Abdourahmane Marieme Sy, 17, and judoka Aicha Diop, 15, jointly carried the final torch, receiving the flame from canoeist Yves Bourhis, triple jumper Sally Sarr and Amadou Dia Ba, Senegal's first and, to date, only Olympic medalist. As the Olympic cauldron was lit, dancers wearing masks and futuristic costumes created a pathway for an Afrofuturism-inspired fashion show. The act also featured a standout performance by a 12-year-old drummer whose solo drew loud applause. At 8:30 p.m., the performers took their final bow, bringing the ceremony to a jubilant close. Held in Dakar, Diamniadio and Saly from Oct. 31 to Nov. 13, the fourth edition of the YOG will bring together more than 2,600 athletes from over 200 delegations. A total of 25 sports will feature on the official competition program, alongside 10 engagement sports. Dakar 2026 will also feature the Youth Olympic debuts of wushu, baseball5 and skateboarding, as well as the Refugee Olympic Team's historic first appearance at the Games. China has sent 66 athletes to compete in 21 sports at the Dakar Youth Olympics. Wushu athlete Lin Yilei and swimmer Chang Mohan, both 15, were named China's flagbearers for the opening ceremony. ■ Artists perform during the opening ceremony of the 2026 Youth Olympic Games in Dakar, Senegal, Oct. 31, 2026. item.title: China's marriage registration innovations boost the "sweet economy"
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-01
* China has allowed couples to complete marriage registration at any qualified civil affairs registry nationwide, making it easier for them to combine registration with travel. * Local governments are improving public services for newlyweds, including premarital health checks, marriage-related legal awareness campaigns and wedding consumption vouchers. * By the end of 2025, China had established 1,330 outdoor sites for certificate presentation and 525 marriage registration sites in parks and other landmark locations. NANJING, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- Since China removed the requirement that couples register their marriages in the locality of their household registration, local authorities across the country have been exploring new venues and services to make the process more personalized and memorable. From tourist destinations to football stadiums, music festivals and university campuses, young couples are choosing venues of marriage registration that reflect their interests and love stories. Also contributing to this trend is the growth of China's wedding industry and a range of government measures to support marriage, childbirth and child-rearing. ROMANTIC MOMENT As a football fan, Wu Jingyu had never imagined that she and her would-be husband would register their marriage outside a football stadium during a match, exchanging vows and receiving their marriage certificate with the roar of the crowd in the background. "It was truly unforgettable. The passion of watching football blended with the joy and romance of getting married," Wu said, recalling the couple's emotional moment outside the home stadium at a recent Jiangsu Football City League match in the city of Wuxi, east China's Jiangsu Province. A photo wall and red ceremonial platform had been set up outside the stadium as a temporary marriage registration venue. Surrounded by cheering fans and family members, couples completed their formalities in a setting far removed from the conventional government service hall. Such arrangements are emerging across China as local authorities seek to meet the preferences of younger couples and give marriage registration a greater sense of occasion. In Nanjing, a city with around 2,500 years of recorded history in Jiangsu, couples interested in traditional culture can wear Han-style wedding robes and phoenix crowns, along with traditional makeup, for their registration ceremony. Other cities have incorporated marriage registration into music festivals, while some universities have organized group wedding ceremonies for alumni returning to their campuses. By the end of 2025, China had established 1,330 outdoor sites for certificate presentation and 525 marriage registration sites in parks and other landmark locations, according to the Ministry of Civil Affairs. "Younger Chinese are exercising greater autonomy in their views on love and marriage," said Zhou Yongbo, a professor at Soochow University in Jiangsu. "They value not only the marriage certificate but also a personalized experience, a sense of ceremony and memories they can cherish." THE "SWEET ECONOMY" Since May 2025, China has allowed couples to complete marriage registration at any qualified civil affairs registry nationwide, making it easier for them to combine registration with travel. In Lijiang, southwest China's Yunnan Province, a couple exchanged vows in front of the snow-capped Yulong Snow Mountain, framed by a heart-shaped arch of white roses. This province's tourism and cut-flower industries give it natural advantages as a destination-wedding choice, and local scenic areas and wedding companies have moved quickly to build a mature industry. Yang Libin, head of a wedding planning company in Yunnan with over a decade of experience, began focusing on customized destination weddings in 2025. His team uses questionnaires and consultations to learn about couples' stories and preferences before selecting venues and designing ceremonies. "Professional services should improve the couples' experience and make every wedding unique," Yang said. In the first year after their shift of focus, his company organized more than 280 destination weddings. The wedding photography industry is another major part of the "sweet economy." In Lijiang, industry associations have introduced service standards covering makeup, clothing, photo production and after-sales support. Packages costing around 10,000 yuan (about 1,500 U.S. dollars) can include costumes, makeup, private transport and accommodation. By integrating photography, ceremonies and honeymoon travel, Lijiang attracted more than 140,000 couples in 2025, with its wedding industry market exceeding 1.1 billion yuan. In Dali, another popular Yunnan destination, businesses have developed over 30 wedding settings, including lakeside lawns and traditional Bai ethnic courtyards, drawing on the area's Cangshan Mountain and Erhai Lake. Wang Yu, a groom from Hebei Province in north China, and his wife held their ceremony in the morning and took wedding photos near Erhai Lake in the afternoon, while relatives and friends visited nearby attractions. "There were no complicated formalities, and we could combine getting married with traveling. It has been a great experience." IMPROVED PUBLIC SERVICES While simplifying registration procedures, local governments are also improving services for newlyweds. In Haidian District of Beijing, for example, its maternal and child health care hospital has set up a premarital health center inside the district's marriage registration office. Newlyweds can complete a premarital health check and marriage registration in the same building and on the same day. In Chengdu, capital of southwest China's Sichuan Province, a team from the local court has worked with marriage registration offices on multiple occasions during peak registration periods, giving newlyweds legal handbooks on marriage and family, Civil Code brochures, and briefings on spousal rights, joint property and family dispute resolution. This effort is part of a broader push to embed legal education into the registration process. Many localities have even introduced marriage incentives and wedding consumption vouchers to help newlyweds manage expenses. Also, many provincial-level regions have extended marriage leave, with the longest reaching 30 days. Local governments are seeking to link the development of the "sweet economy" with efforts to create a more supportive environment for marriage, childbirth and child-rearing. In 2025, China introduced 23 measures to support childbirth and child-rearing. Multiple regions have made childbirth-related medical expenses largely or entirely free for families, while Jiangsu has introduced childcare service vouchers. Zhou added that localities are pairing the new registration settings with premarital education and legal consultation, which helps young people understand the rights and obligations of marriage and avoid registering on impulse. "The business of romance is closely connected to people's aspirations for a better life," he said. "As society places greater emphasis on creating a family-friendly environment, preserving that sweetness requires continued innovation in public services." ■

item.title: World Insights: Yerevan Pathway charts course for biodiversity action, but challenges remain
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-01
YEREVAN, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- The 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17) concluded in Yerevan on Saturday after negotiators secured agreement on the conference's main decisions, including the Yerevan Pathway aimed at accelerating global biodiversity action. This encouraging outcome came at a critical time for global biodiversity protection. Halfway between the adoption of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework and its 2030 deadline, countries face a widening gap between their commitments to protect nature and the action to fulfill them. Whether the Yerevan Pathway can help close that gap will depend on financing, national policies and sustained international cooperation. A PATHWAY TO ACCELERATE ACTION The conference's main task was to conduct the first global review of collective progress in implementing the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, which sets out 23 targets for 2030. The assessment presented governments with a clear warning: Without a rapid acceleration of implementation, the framework's 2030 targets and mission would not be achieved, putting its longer-term goals for 2050 at risk. The Yerevan Pathway is part of the response to that assessment. Rather than setting new targets, it focuses on how countries can step up efforts to meet those already agreed upon. Embedded in the global review decision, the pathway identifies several priorities for the period through 2030: accelerating implementation, broadening the coverage of national targets, strengthening financial and other support, engaging governments and societies more widely, and improving monitoring and knowledge. Negotiators also adopted decisions covering protected areas and forest biodiversity, sustainable wildlife management, invasive alien species, marine and coastal biodiversity, synthetic biology and other areas. Alongside the negotiations, nearly 2 billion U.S. dollars in new biodiversity funding was announced, according to the Secretariat of the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD). This included 560 million dollars under the ninth replenishment of the Global Environment Facility and its Global Biodiversity Framework Fund, 500 million dollars through the Species Recovery Alliance, and more than 330 million dollars through the Value Nature Fund. Together, the decisions and funding announcements provide a basis for further action. However, the effectiveness of the pathway will depend on whether international agreements lead to changes in national priorities and concrete action on the ground. FINANCE DIVIDE TESTS DELIVERY Finance remains one of the main obstacles to implementation, both in terms of how much funding is available and how the responsibility for providing it is shared. The global report found that developed countries had failed to meet their commitment to provide at least 20 billion dollars annually in biodiversity finance to developing countries by 2025. This shortfall was a major point of contention in negotiations over funding for the next stage of implementation. Some developed countries called for broadening the contributor base, bringing into focus a longstanding dispute over the relationship between countries' financial capacity and their obligations under the CBD. Article 20 of the convention requires developed-country parties to provide new and additional financial resources, while allowing other parties to assume such obligations voluntarily. The new funding announcements offered some encouragement, but the broader challenge of securing predictable support on the scale needed remains. For developing countries, efforts to strengthen conservation, restore ecosystems and monitor progress continue to depend heavily on access to finance and technical assistance. Nor did the conference resolve every issue. Negotiations on cooperation and strategic review, along with two items under the Nagoya Protocol, remained unfinished and were deferred to the next ordinary meetings. "Every diluted clause, every deferred target, is a step towards irreversible loss," Guido Broekhoven, interim global director of multilateral policy at the World Wide Fund for Nature International, told a press conference before the closing session. His remarks underscored a central challenge facing the negotiations: while consensus is essential to international cooperation, biodiversity loss continues as governments work to reach agreement. CHINA'S ROLE IN ADVANCING IMPLEMENTATION Turning commitments into concrete results was also a key theme in discussions of China's contribution, including its support for the global review, sharing experience in domestic conservation and financing for biodiversity projects in developing countries. The global review decision specifically thanked China for hosting the Kunming dialogue to support preparations for the review. It also acknowledged financial support provided through the China Trust Fund via the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP). In an interview with Xinhua during the conference, COP17 President Hambardzum Matevosyan said China had made important contributions to advancing the talks, from preparatory work to the formal negotiations. Such cooperation has practical relevance as countries seek ways to overcome implementation barriers, Matevosyan said, adding that national experiences can help identify approaches that others may adapt to their own circumstances. Astrid Schomaker, executive secretary of the secretariat of the CBD, said the progress reflected in China's seventh national report was encouraging and highlighted its ecological conservation red lines as an example of how biodiversity protection could be incorporated into national planning and development. Financial support is another important part of turning the framework into action. Inger Andersen, executive director of the UNEP, recognized China's continued leadership through the establishment of the Kunming Biodiversity Fund following its COP15 presidency. She emphasized the importance of helping developing countries access the financing needed to implement the agreement. These contributions point to the task now facing all parties: ensuring that international cooperation is backed by the funding, institutions and policies needed to deliver results. The Yerevan conference preserved a common direction at a difficult moment for biodiversity protection. The next four years will determine whether governments can turn their commitments into measurable progress before the 2030 deadline. As Schomaker put it: "Ultimately, the test is not what governments agreed in Yerevan, but what they change when they return home."■

item.title: China Focus: Face up to responsibility for invading China -- a call from a Japanese delegation
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-01
Members of a Japanese delegation from the Association for Inheriting and Propagating the Murayama Statement visit the former site of Unit 731 in Harbin, northeast China's Heilongjiang Province, Oct. 28, 2026. (Xinhua/He Shan) HARBIN, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- In late autumn, members of a Japanese delegation stood with solemn expressions in extended silence at an exhibition hall presenting evidence of crimes committed by the notorious biological warfare division Unit 731 of invading Japanese troops during World War II. In recent days, the Japanese civil-society delegation visited the exhibition hall and former sites of Unit 731 in northeast China's Heilongjiang Province. During the visit, the delegation took the opportunity to exchange views with Chinese experts and scholars. The delegation is from the Association for Inheriting and Propagating the Murayama Statement, which was established in Tokyo, Japan, in 2013. Composed of scholars, journalists, lawyers, and civic activists, it is a progressive force within Japan that persists in reflecting on the history of aggression. Shigenori Kanehira, a delegation member and veteran Japanese media professional, said that although he already knew a lot about this history, stepping into these historical sites in person left him even more shocked. Mitsuhisa Fukutomi, another delegation member and a university professor, expressed a similar sentiment. A scholar who has long taught international politics, he was somewhat familiar with the crimes of Unit 731, yet he still felt immense shame and sorrow upon seeing these crime scenes firsthand. The visit helped the delegation fully recognize that the truth could not be buried, despite the invading Japanese troops' deliberate destruction of core facilities in an attempt to conceal evidence of their crimes. Decades of archaeological excavations and academic verification have established an irrefutable chain of criminal evidence beyond doubt. After visiting a human experiment exhibition area, Takakage Fujita, head of the delegation, said the Japanese army's act of injecting bacteria into living people can only be described as "demonic." "As a Japanese, I sincerely apologize to the Chinese people who perished in the disaster," he added. During a symposium with experts and scholars from the exhibition hall, Fujita strongly condemned the growing tide of historical revisionism and right-wing countercurrents in Japan in recent years. He noted that since last year, some right-wing politicians in Japan have openly made absurd and ignorant remarks in attempts to incite regional conflict, even brazenly clamoring that the war of aggression was a "war of self-defense" and a "just war," which is utterly outrageous. The delegation agreed that post-war right-wing forces in Japan deliberately played down the history of aggression and revised textbooks, leaving Japan's younger generation with a serious lack of understanding of the history of aggression against China. Such state-driven historical erasure is precisely the soil in which the rampant right-wing ideology in Japanese society today has taken root. Despite years of sustained pressure from right-wing forces in Japan, concerned people in China and Japan have never wavered in their efforts to preserve historical truth. Jin Chengmin, an expert with the exhibition hall, said at the symposium that over the years, people-to-people exchanges among scholars, journalists, lawyers and civil-society groups in China and Japan have served as a bridge for rational communication and a shared understanding of history between the two countries. After the symposium concluded, Jin donated a photocopy of a handwritten letter former Japanese Prime Minister Tomiichi Murayama left during his 2007 visit to China to the Association for Inheriting and Propagating the Murayama Statement. The letter bears the inscription "Learn from history and open up a future of peace and friendship between Japan and China." "Those responsible for the war committed heinous atrocities, yet went on to live out their postwar years in comfort. This is an unacceptable failure of justice," said Fujita. He added that the delegation will continue to pursue accountability for war responsibility within Japan, counter historical nihilism, and promote China-Japan friendship as it is the only correct path to peace and prosperity for both countries. ■ Members of a Japanese delegation from the Association for Inheriting and Propagating the Murayama Statement visit the former site of Unit 731 in Harbin, northeast China's Heilongjiang Province, Oct. 28, 2026. (Xinhua/Yang Siqi)

item.title: China's new rules to protect children's health, safety take effect
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-01
BEIJING, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- Four new or revised mandatory national standards and regulations to better protect children's health and safety took effect in China on Sunday, covering classroom lighting, youth sports training, and children's products and toys. The rules aim to reduce health and safety risks in children's daily learning, physical activities and play, with a greater emphasis on prevention and clearer safety requirements. BETTER LIGHTING TO PROTECT EYESIGHT A revised national standard on classroom lighting and daylighting sets stricter requirements for the lighting environment in primary and secondary schools, as China steps up efforts to curb myopia among children and adolescents. The standard addresses aspects such as natural light, lighting uniformity, blue-light hazards and flicker, aiming to enhance the comfort of classrooms for students who spend long hours reading and writing. It also calls for regular inspections and upkeep of lighting equipment. The revised standard will also apply to secondary vocational schools, while extracurricular training institutions serving school-age children are encouraged to follow its requirements. Liu Yiwei, a lecturer at Capital Normal University, said the new standard sets more detailed mandatory requirements for classroom lighting, providing a measurable and enforceable framework to support efforts to prevent myopia among young students. It incorporates the principle of putting health first into educational settings and places greater emphasis on preventing myopia before it develops, Liu added. MORE STANDARDIZED SPORTS TRAINING A new code of conduct for youth sports training sets requirements for training venues, class sizes, instructor qualifications and safety management, addressing concerns over unsafe facilities and uneven coaching standards in a rapidly growing market. It is essential for training providers to tailor courses to align with the ages, physical conditions, and varying levels of athletic ability of children. Instructors must hold recognized qualifications, while people with specified criminal records, including those involving sexual abuse or physical assault, are prohibited from working in the sector. The rules also establish limits on class sizes and require additional first-aid support for high-risk sports, helping create safer conditions for children to participate in physical activities. Huang Haiyan, dean of the School of Management at Beijing Sport University, noted that the code upgrades the regulatory framework and is a necessary step toward higher-quality development of the industry. The code should serve as a basis for further clarifying the respective oversight responsibilities of education, market regulation and public security authorities, helping improve the overall governance of the industry, Huang said. SAFER CHILDREN'S PRODUCTS, TOYS A new mandatory national standard on the general safety of children's products establishes baseline requirements for products used, worn or played with by children under 14, covering product categories that previously lacked mandatory safety standards. The standard covers risks such as sharp edges, detachable small parts that could cause choking, and cords that could pose strangulation hazards. It also sets limits on potentially harmful chemicals, including heavy metals and formaldehyde. Meanwhile, revised mandatory toy safety standards expand controls on hazardous substances and strengthen requirements concerning physical safety and fire risks. The revisions pay particular attention to products that have drawn public concern, including popular novelty toys such as squishy toys and slime. They introduce additional limits on substances such as formaldehyde, plasticizers and boron, helping reduce the risk of harmful chemical exposure. Together, the new requirements are the country's latest move to fill the safety gaps for certain products used in children's everyday lives, making safety standards more comprehensive as the range of children's goods continues to expand. ■

item.title: Protocol upgrading China-Peru FTA takes effect
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-01
BEIJING, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- The protocol upgrading the China-Peru free trade agreement (FTA) took effect on Sunday, according to China's Ministry of Commerce (MOC). China and Peru launched negotiations on the upgrade in November 2018 and signed the protocol on Nov. 14, 2024. The original FTA was signed in 2009 and took effect in 2010. The protocol improves seven existing chapters of the original FTA, covering rules of origin, customs procedures and trade facilitation, sanitary and phytosanitary measures, intellectual property rights, trade in services, temporary entry of business personnel, and investment, the MOC said in an online statement. The protocol also adds five new chapters on standards and conformity assessment cooperation, competition policy, e-commerce, global supply chains, and environment and trade. The two sides also set out future provisions for negotiations on negative lists for trade in services and investment, aimed at further raising openness in these areas, according to the statement. The China-Peru FTA was the first comprehensive free trade agreement China signed with a Latin American country. China is Peru's largest trading partner, largest export market and largest source of imports, while Peru is China's fourth-largest trading partner in Latin America and an important investment destination, said an MOC official. Under the protocol, the new chapter on global supply chains encourages multimodal transport and the development of foreign trade logistics corridors and infrastructure, an innovative arrangement that signals the two countries' commitment to keeping supply chains stable and unimpeded. The chapter on standards and conformity assessment cooperation establishes a dedicated cooperation mechanism and sets out an intended cooperation list, creating a platform for mutual recognition of standards that is expected to reduce trade costs for enterprises. The two sides agreed to launch negotiations on negative lists for trade in services and investment within two years after the protocol takes effect, in a bid to further raise the level of openness in these areas and continue to tap the potential of bilateral trade and investment, the official added. Since the original FTA came into force in 2010, it has played an important role in promoting bilateral economic and trade cooperation. Two-way trade rose from 6.4 billion U.S. dollars in 2009 to 50.4 billion U.S. dollars in 2025, an increase of nearly seven times, official data show. The protocol is expected to help tap further opportunities for bilateral trade and investment cooperation, provide a better business environment for enterprises of both countries and inject new vitality into bilateral economic and trade relations, the MOC said. ■

item.title: Political party leaders worldwide laud 5th plenary session of 20th CPC Central Committee
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-01
BEIJING, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- Leaders of political parties around the world have extended congratulations on the successful convening of the fifth plenary session of the 20th Central Committee of the Communist Party of China (CPC). They spoke highly of the CPC's experience and achievements in persistently advancing full and rigorous Party self-governance, and highly appreciated the important insights that Xi Jinping Thought on Party Building offers for the development of political parties around the world. Abhisit Vejjajiva, leader of Thailand's Democrat Party and former Thai prime minister, said that the CPC has accurately grasped major trends in global development and responded to the fundamental demands of the people. The CPC's governance practices and valuable experience offer valuable lessons and are worthy of serious reflection by other political parties, he said. Madhav Kumar Nepal, co-coordinator of the Nepali Communist Party and former Nepali prime minister, said Xi Jinping Thought on Party Building has answered questions that all political parties must confront but few have seriously addressed. Only by consistently attaching great importance to party building and having the courage to renew itself can a political party lead a country toward lasting peace and stability, he said. Luther Tarpeh, national chairman of the Unity Party of Liberia, said the CPC's successful governance model has paved the way for national rejuvenation with sustainable development, offering valuable lessons for the Global South countries. Sophia Shaningwa, secretary general of Namibia's South West Africa People's Organization (SWAPO) party, said that Xi Jinping, general secretary of the CPC Central Committee, has offered an effective solution to address the issue of party governance. SWAPO is willing to enhance exchanges and mutual learning with the CPC, and systematically study Xi Jinping Thought on Party Building, she said. Asha-Rose Migiro, secretary-general of Tanzania's Chama Cha Mapinduzi party, said that this meeting will consolidate the institutional foundation for Chinese modernization and the successful implementation of the 15th Five-Year Plan for National Economic and Social Development. Richard Todwong, secretary-general of Uganda's National Resistance Movement, said the CPC's efforts to strengthen party building have provided strong support for realizing Chinese modernization while offering a valuable model for developing countries, including those in Africa, to enhance their governance capacity. Dmitry Novikov, deputy chairman of the Central Committee of the Communist Party of the Russian Federation and first deputy chairman of the State Duma Committee on International Affairs, said what makes the CPC great is its ability to engage in self-reflection, face problems head-on and take action to address them, which ensures that power is exercised to serve the people rather than private interests and that the party maintains vitality and dynamism. In doing so, the CPC has set an example for political parties in other countries, he said. ■

item.title: Full text: Resolution of the Central Committee of the Communist Party of China on Certain Major Issues concerning Persevering with Full and Rigorous Party Self-Governance

item.title: China's "porcelain capital" wins Global Award for Sustainable Development in Cities
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-31
FUZHOU, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- The global observance of 2026 World Cities Day was held on Saturday in east China's Fuzhou, with five cities, including China's "porcelain capital" Jingdezhen, honored with the fourth-cycle Global Award for Sustainable Development in Cities, also known as the Shanghai Award. The event runs from Oct. 31 to Nov. 2. Apart from Jingdezhen, the other four recipients of the Shanghai Award, which recognizes cities for achievements in sustainable urban development, are Addis Ababa in Ethiopia, Santiago de Cali in Colombia, Istanbul in Türkiye, and Katowice in Poland. The event brings together senior United Nations officials alongside representatives from national governments, local authorities, international organizations, academic institutions, the private sector, and community networks to share best practices and advance practical solutions to common urban challenges. In December 2013, the 68th United Nations General Assembly adopted a resolution designating Oct. 31 as World Cities Day starting in 2014. It was the first international day proposed by the Chinese government at the United Nations. Ceramic culture has long been an ideal medium for cross-civilization dialogue. As a cornerstone commodity of the ancient Silk Road, Jingdezhen porcelain was a defining cultural symbol, through which the world came to know China and China reached out to the world. Building on this legacy, Jingdezhen has embraced a model of development that combines cultural preservation with creative renewal. Former porcelain factories have been reimagined as cultural and creative districts, old streets are lined with ceramic-themed installations, and historic neighborhoods have been carefully preserved and revitalized. The city is home to more than 3,200 inheritors of intangible cultural heritage in ceramic craftsmanship. It has also been named in the UNESCO Creative Cities Network as a City of Crafts and Folk Art. Jingdezhen's recognition is just one example of China's broader urban renewal efforts. Urban renewal also holds huge potential for investment and consumption. China has set a target of renovating 1,500 old streets and factory compounds from 2026 to 2030, bringing in new industries and business models to inject fresh momentum into urban development. "Converting old streets and factory sites into cultural and creative districts drives growth in dining, retail and entertainment," said Yan Yuejin, deputy director of the E-house China R&D Institute. ■
